title: Portfolio Management Services (PMS) Distributors
blurb: What distributors need to know to offer portfolio management services: how PMS works, who it suits, how it is measured, taxed and regulated.

units.title: Investments
units.overview: The language of investing: asset classes, risk, return and the time value of money. Foundation for every later unit.
facts: Asset class
An asset class is a group of investments with similar characteristics, such as equity, fixed income, gold and real estate.
An investor splits money between shares, bonds and gold.
Equity and debt are the same asset class.
Risk and return
Higher expected return generally requires acceptance of higher risk; investors are paid for bearing risk.
A client chasing higher returns must accept larger swings.
High return can be earned without any added risk.
Time value of money
Money received sooner is worth more than the same sum later because it can earn a return.
₹1 crore today is worth more than ₹1 crore in five years.
The time value of money is the interest on a loan.
Compounding
Compounding generates returns on past returns, growing wealth faster over long horizons.
Reinvested gains themselves earn further gains.
Compounding means returns on the initial sum only.
Inflation
Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money; real return is nominal return minus inflation, approximately.
A 10% return with 6% inflation yields about 4% real return.
Inflation raises the real return of cash.
Risk types
Investment risks include market, credit, liquidity, interest-rate and concentration risks.
A concentrated portfolio suffers when its top holding falls.
Concentration risk applies only to bonds.
Risk profile
A client's risk profile combines willingness and ability to bear loss and guides the portfolio mix.
A client with a short horizon and low tolerance has a conservative profile.
Risk profile is irrelevant to PMS.
Diversification
Diversification spreads investments across securities and asset classes to reduce specific risk.
A portfolio holding 25 stocks across sectors.
Diversification removes all risk.
Investment horizon
The investment horizon is the period for which funds can remain invested, affecting what assets are suitable.
A client who needs funds in 6 months has a short horizon.
Horizon has no effect on asset choice.

units.title: Introduction to securities markets
units.overview: The markets in which portfolio managers operate and the regulators who oversee them.
facts: Primary market
The primary market is where securities are first issued to investors and the issuer receives the proceeds.
An IPO raises funds for a company.
Investors trade with each other in the primary market.
Secondary market
The secondary market is where existing securities trade between investors on exchanges, providing liquidity.
An investor sells shares through a stock exchange.
The company receives funds from secondary market trades.
Stock exchange
A stock exchange is a regulated platform where listed securities trade, such as the BSE and NSE.
Buyers and sellers meet on an electronic platform.
A stock exchange issues shares to the public.
Depository
A depository holds securities in electronic form, enabling transfer by book entry; India has NSDL and CDSL.
A client's shares are held electronically in a demat account.
A depository sets stock prices.
SEBI
SEBI regulates the securities market including portfolio managers, and frames regulations to protect investors.
A portfolio manager must register with the capital-market regulator.
SEBI regulates only banks.
Settlement
Equity trades settle on T+1 through a clearing corporation, which guarantees settlement.
Shares bought today are delivered the next working day.
Equity trades take a week to settle.

units.title: Investing in stocks
units.overview: How portfolio managers analyse and select equity investments: valuation, style and risk.
focus: Growth versus value; large versus small.
facts: Equity share
An equity share represents ownership in a company with a residual claim on profits and assets.
A client owns part of a listed company.
Equity gives a fixed return.
Market capitalisation
Market capitalisation is share price times shares outstanding, used to classify companies as large, mid or small cap.
A company with 10 crore shares at ₹300 is valued at ₹3,000 crore.
Market cap is the company's debt.
Price-to-earnings ratio
P/E is the share price divided by earnings per share, showing how much investors pay per rupee of earnings.
A stock at ₹300 with EPS of ₹15 has a P/E of 20.
P/E is earnings divided by price.
Price-to-book ratio
P/B compares share price with book value per share, widely used for banks and asset-heavy companies.
A bank at ₹300 with book value of ₹150 trades at 2 times.
P/B compares price with dividend.
Return on equity
ROE is net profit divided by shareholders' equity and measures how effectively equity is used.
A company earns ₹20 crore on equity of ₹100 crore.
ROE is price divided by earnings.
Growth investing
Growth investing seeks companies with above-average earnings growth, often at higher valuations.
A manager buys fast-growing firms with premium multiples.
Growth investors buy only stocks with the lowest P/E.
Value investing
Value investing buys stocks trading below estimated intrinsic value, expecting the price to converge.
A manager buys a good business at a low multiple.
Value investors buy only the most expensive stocks.
Quality investing
Quality investing favours companies with high returns on capital, stable earnings and strong governance.
A manager picks businesses with durable returns and low debt.
Quality investing seeks the most indebted firms.
Large, mid and small caps
Large caps are generally more stable and liquid; small caps offer higher growth potential with more volatility and lower liquidity.
A small-cap stock falls sharply on a bad quarter.
Small caps are less volatile than large caps.
Dividend
A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders, which forms part of total return along with price change.
A company pays ₹6 per share to holders.
Dividends are guaranteed every year.
Equity risks
Equity investors face market, company-specific, valuation and liquidity risks, and can lose capital.
A stock falls 40% after a profit warning.
Equity cannot lose capital over short periods.
Sector concentration
Concentrating a portfolio in one sector raises risk because sector-specific shocks hit all holdings together.
A portfolio holding mostly banking stocks falls when banks fall.
Sector concentration lowers portfolio risk.
Corporate governance
Good governance, with independent boards and transparent disclosure, reduces the risk of value loss to minority shareholders.
A manager avoids a company with weak disclosure.
Governance does not affect investment risk.

units.title: Investing in fixed income securities
units.overview: Bonds and debt instruments in a portfolio: yield, duration and credit.
facts: Bond
A bond is a debt instrument paying periodic interest (coupon) and repaying principal at maturity.
An investor lends to a company and receives coupons.
A bond gives ownership in the company.
Coupon and yield
The coupon is the fixed interest on face value, while yield is the return based on current price; yield rises when price falls.
A bond bought below face value yields more than its coupon.
Yield and price move in the same direction.
Duration
Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest-rate changes; higher duration means larger price swings.
A long bond falls more than a short one when rates rise.
Duration is the bond's maturity date.
Credit risk
Credit risk is the possibility that the issuer fails to pay interest or principal on time.
A bond rated BBB is more exposed than one rated AAA.
Government bonds carry the highest credit risk.
Credit rating
A credit rating is an agency's opinion of an issuer's ability to repay, from AAA (highest) downward.
A bond is rated AA+ by a rating agency.
A credit rating is a guarantee of repayment.
Government security
A G-sec is issued by the government with negligible credit risk, though price changes with yields.
A manager holds G-secs for safety and liquidity.
G-secs have no price risk.
Money market instruments
Money market instruments mature within a year and are used to park short-term funds.
A portfolio holds T-bills for liquidity.
Money market instruments mature in 10 years.

units.title: Derivatives
units.overview: Derivatives in portfolios: hedging and the risks of leverage.
facts: Derivative
A derivative is a contract whose value depends on an underlying asset, such as a share or an index.
A contract based on the Nifty 50.
A derivative has no link to any underlying.
Futures
A futures contract is an exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date.
A manager sells index futures to hedge a portfolio.
Futures give a right without an obligation.
Options
An option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a fixed price for a premium.
A manager buys a put to protect a position.
An option obliges the buyer to complete the trade.
Hedging
Hedging uses derivatives to offset an existing risk, reducing the portfolio's exposure to adverse moves.
A manager protects holdings with a put option.
Hedging aims to increase risk.
Leverage risk
Derivatives allow large exposure for small margin, magnifying gains and losses.
A small price move leads to a large loss on margin.
Leverage reduces risk.

units.title: Collective investment vehicles
units.overview: Mutual funds, ETFs and AIFs compared with PMS.
visuals: Each trade taxed in client's hands
facts: Mutual fund
A mutual fund pools money from many investors into a scheme managed by an AMC, with investors owning units.
Investors hold units in a pooled scheme.
A mutual fund holds each investor's securities separately.
ETF
An ETF is a fund traded on exchanges, typically tracking an index at low cost.
An investor buys units of a fund like a share.
An ETF is bought only from the AMC at NAV.
Alternative investment fund
An AIF is a privately pooled vehicle for sophisticated investors with a minimum of ₹1 crore.
An investor commits ₹1 crore to a private equity fund.
An AIF accepts small retail investments.
PMS versus mutual fund
In PMS, securities are held in the client's own account and each trade is tax-relevant for the client; in mutual funds, investors hold pooled units.
A PMS client's demat shows the underlying shares.
In PMS, assets are pooled with other clients' money.
NAV
NAV is the per-unit value of a scheme, equal to net assets divided by units outstanding.
A scheme's value per unit is ₹40.
NAV is used to value a PMS client's individual holdings.
Expense versus fee
Mutual funds charge an expense ratio inside NAV, while PMS charges management and performance fees separately to the client.
A PMS client is billed management fee and performance fee.
PMS has no fees.
Transparency
PMS clients see their own holdings and transactions, while mutual fund investors see a pooled portfolio.
A PMS client checks each stock in her own portfolio.
PMS clients cannot see holdings.

units.title: Role of portfolio managers
units.overview: What a portfolio manager does and the three types of service.
facts: Portfolio manager
A portfolio manager is a SEBI-registered body corporate that manages or administers a client's securities or funds under a contract.
A registered firm invests a client's money under a signed agreement.
A portfolio manager can be an unregistered individual.
Discretionary PMS
In discretionary PMS the manager takes investment decisions independently on behalf of the client, without asking approval for each trade.
A manager buys and sells for the client based on the strategy without consent.
In discretionary PMS the client approves every trade.
Non-discretionary PMS
In non-discretionary PMS the manager advises and executes only after the client's prior approval for each decision.
A manager proposes a trade and executes it after the client agrees.
The manager decides without consulting the client.
Advisory PMS
In advisory PMS the manager only advises; the client decides and executes.
The client acts on the manager's recommendation herself.
The advisory manager executes trades for the client.
Minimum investment
A client's minimum investment with a portfolio manager is ₹50 lakh, in funds or securities, with a lower threshold for accredited investors.
A client must commit at least ₹50 lakh.
PMS accepts investments of ₹5 lakh from retail clients.
Investment approach
An investment approach is a distinct style or strategy offered by a portfolio manager, such as large-cap growth or multi-cap value, with defined objectives and risks.
A manager offers a quality-focused multi-cap approach.
An investment approach is a promise of returns.
Client's own account
Securities in a PMS are held in a separate demat account in the client's name, giving ownership and transparency.
A client's shares appear in her own demat account.
PMS pools all client money into one demat account.
Distributor's role
A PMS distributor introduces the service to clients, explains the product, assesses suitability and receives commission as per regulations.
A certified distributor evaluates whether a client fits a PMS.
A distributor manages the client's portfolio.
Direct onboarding
Clients have the option to be onboarded directly with the portfolio manager without a distributor, and the manager must offer a direct plan.
A client approaches the manager directly and avoids distribution commission.
Clients can invest in PMS only through distributors.
Registration of portfolio managers
Portfolio managers must be registered with SEBI and meet net-worth requirements; the minimum net worth is ₹5 crore.
A firm with insufficient net worth cannot be registered.
Portfolio managers need no minimum net worth.
Investor charter
Portfolio managers must provide an investor charter explaining the rights and obligations of clients and the grievance process.
A client receives a document describing her rights.
Investor charters are optional.
Segregation of client assets
Client assets must be kept separate from the manager's own assets, with a custodian required for safekeeping.
A custodian holds the securities of PMS clients separately.
A manager may hold client assets alongside its own.
Limits on pooling
A portfolio manager cannot pool client funds the way a mutual fund does; each client's portfolio is managed individually.
Each client's holdings are separate in a PMS account.
PMS invests all client money in a single pool.

units.title: Operational aspects of portfolio managers
units.overview: How a PMS actually operates: agreements, onboarding, fees, custody and reporting.
facts: Portfolio management agreement
The agreement between manager and client sets out services, fees, rights, risks, and termination terms, and is mandatory.
A client signs a detailed contract before investing.
A PMS can start without a written agreement.
Disclosure document
The disclosure document gives the client full information about the manager, investment approach, fees, risks and litigation before signing.
A client receives a document describing the manager and charges before investing.
The disclosure document is given after the first year.
Fixed fee
A fixed management fee is charged as a percentage of assets irrespective of performance.
A manager charges 2% of assets every year.
A fixed fee depends on profits.
Return-based fee
A return-based fee is charged only on profits above a hurdle rate, subject to a high-water mark.
The manager earns a share only of returns above 10%.
A return-based fee is charged even if the portfolio loses money.
Hybrid fee
A hybrid fee combines a lower fixed fee with a performance fee.
A manager charges 1% of assets plus 10% of profits above a hurdle.
A hybrid fee has no fixed component.
Hurdle rate
A hurdle rate is the minimum return the portfolio must earn before a performance fee is charged.
The manager earns a fee only when returns exceed 8%.
A hurdle rate is the maximum fee permitted.
High-water mark
The high-water mark is the highest value of the portfolio on which a performance fee was last paid; a new fee is charged only on gains above it.
After a loss, no performance fee is charged until the value exceeds the previous peak.
A high-water mark resets every month.
Exit load
Exit load is a charge on withdrawal in the early years: at most 3% in the first year, 2% in the second and 1% in the third, with none thereafter.
A client who exits early pays a decreasing charge.
Exit load is the same in every year.
Custodian
A custodian safekeeps the securities of PMS clients independent of the manager, and settles trades.
An independent institution holds client assets.
The portfolio manager acts as the sole custodian.
Client reporting
Managers must give clients periodic reports showing portfolio holdings, transactions, performance and charges.
A client receives a quarterly report on holdings and returns.
Managers need not report to clients.
Contribution of securities
Clients may contribute securities instead of cash, and the manager may hold them or realign the portfolio, with tax consequences.
A client transfers existing shares to start a PMS.
Clients can contribute only cash.
Termination
Either party may terminate the agreement as per its terms, usually with notice; assets are returned in the form specified.
A client withdraws from the service as the contract allows.
A client cannot leave the PMS before 10 years.
Withdrawals and partial redemptions
Clients may withdraw funds or securities as per the agreement, with notice and exit load as applicable.
A client takes out part of the portfolio and bears any exit load.
Partial withdrawals are never allowed.
Brokerage and expenses
Brokerage and other expenses on transactions, such as custodian and audit fees, are charged to the client as disclosed.
A client's statement shows brokerage and custodian charges.
Costs are not passed to PMS clients.
Audit and compliance
Portfolio managers are subject to annual audits and reporting to SEBI, and must have compliance officers.
A firm's compliance is audited each year.
Portfolio managers are never audited.
Conflict of interest
Managers must avoid and disclose conflicts, such as trading in the same securities for own account ahead of clients.
A manager discloses related-party trades.
Conflicts need not be disclosed.

units.title: Portfolio management process
units.overview: The core method: objectives, asset allocation, security selection, implementation and review. The heaviest unit.
facts: Investment objective
The investment objective states what the portfolio is meant to achieve, such as growth, income or capital preservation, with risk and time limits.
A client wants long-term growth with moderate risk.
The investment objective is unrelated to the client's needs.
Investment policy
The investment policy records objectives, constraints, allocation ranges and rebalancing rules, guiding the manager.
A document sets limits on equity and single-stock exposure.
An investment policy is a guarantee of returns.
Constraints
Constraints such as liquidity needs, time horizon, tax, legal limits and unique preferences shape what the portfolio can hold.
A client who needs cash in two years cannot hold illiquid assets.
Constraints do not apply to portfolio construction.
Strategic asset allocation
Strategic allocation sets long-term target weights across asset classes, based on objectives and risk profile.
A portfolio aims for 70% equity and 30% debt over the long term.
Strategic allocation changes every day.
Tactical asset allocation
Tactical allocation makes temporary deviations from the strategic weights to benefit from expected short-term moves.
A manager temporarily cuts equity in an expensive market.
Tactical allocation is a permanent allocation.
Top-down approach
The top-down approach starts with economy and sector views and then selects stocks within favoured sectors.
A manager picks sectors first and then stocks.
A top-down approach starts with individual stocks.
Bottom-up approach
The bottom-up approach starts with analysing individual companies, regardless of macro or sector views.
A manager chooses strong businesses one by one.
A bottom-up approach begins with the macro view.
Active management
Active management seeks to outperform a benchmark through selection and timing decisions, at higher cost.
A manager tries to beat the index through stock selection.
Active managers track the index exactly.
Passive management
Passive management replicates an index at low cost, without attempting to outperform.
A portfolio mirrors the benchmark.
Passive managers pick stocks they expect to beat the market.
Rebalancing
Rebalancing returns the portfolio to its target weights by selling what has risen and buying what has fallen.
Equity drifts above target, so the manager trims it.
Rebalancing means adding to the best performers.
Position sizing
Position sizing sets how much of the portfolio is placed in each security, balancing conviction and risk.
A manager limits any single stock to 10% of the portfolio.
Every holding must be of equal size.
Concentrated portfolio
A concentrated portfolio holds few stocks, offering higher potential returns with higher risk.
A PMS holds 15 stocks.
A concentrated portfolio holds hundreds of stocks.
Portfolio turnover
Portfolio turnover measures how much of the portfolio is bought and sold in a year; high turnover raises costs and taxes.
A manager that trades heavily incurs higher charges.
Turnover has no effect on costs.
Cash in the portfolio
Holding cash gives liquidity and flexibility but can drag returns in rising markets.
A manager keeps 8% in cash for opportunities.
Cash always improves returns.
Stop-loss and risk limits
Risk limits such as stop-losses, single-stock caps and sector caps control downside and discipline.
A manager sells a position when it falls to a pre-set level.
Risk limits are unnecessary for skilled managers.
Behavioural biases
Biases like overconfidence, herding and loss aversion lead to poor decisions; a disciplined process counters them.
A manager sticks to the process despite market noise.
Professional managers are immune to bias.
Suitability for PMS
PMS suits investors with large surplus funds, long horizons and ability to bear volatility and concentration risk.
A high-net-worth client with a ten-year horizon is a candidate.
PMS suits investors needing money in a month.
Tax-aware management
Because each trade is taxed in the client's hands, managers consider holding period and tax impact when trading.
A manager avoids selling just before a gain becomes long-term.
Tax does not affect PMS decisions.
Review and monitoring
The portfolio is reviewed regularly against objectives, benchmark and risk limits, and changes are made as needed.
A manager reviews performance every quarter and discusses with the client.
A PMS portfolio is never reviewed once built.

units.title: Performance measurement and evaluation of portfolio managers
units.overview: How to judge a PMS: returns, benchmarks, risk-adjusted measures and standard reporting.
visuals: TWRR = (1 + R1) × (1 + R2) × ... − 1, where each R is a sub-period return between cash flows
facts: Time-weighted return
TWRR removes the effect of cash inflows and outflows, so it measures the manager's skill independent of the client's timing.
A manager's return is computed between each deposit or withdrawal and then chained.
TWRR is affected by when the client adds money.
Money-weighted return
The money-weighted return (IRR) reflects the size and timing of cash flows and captures the client's actual experience.
A client's own return depends on when she invested.
Money-weighted return ignores cash flow timing.
Annualised return
Annualised return converts a return over any period into an equivalent yearly rate for comparison.
A 21% return over two years is about 10% a year.
Annualised return is the simple sum of all returns.
Benchmark
A benchmark is a standard index against which performance is compared, chosen to match the strategy.
A large-cap portfolio is compared to a large-cap index.
Any index can serve as the benchmark.
Alpha
Alpha is the excess return of a portfolio over its benchmark or over what its risk would predict.
A portfolio earns 3% more than the benchmark.
Alpha is the portfolio's total return.
Standard deviation
Standard deviation measures the volatility of returns; higher values indicate more risk.
A portfolio's returns vary widely from month to month.
Standard deviation measures the average return.
Sharpe ratio
The Sharpe ratio measures excess return per unit of total risk; a higher ratio means better risk-adjusted performance.
Two managers with equal returns are compared on risk taken.
The Sharpe ratio considers only returns.
Maximum drawdown
Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough decline in portfolio value, showing worst-case loss experienced.
A portfolio fell 30% from its highest value.
Maximum drawdown measures the biggest gain.
Up and down capture
Capture ratios show how much of the benchmark's up and down moves a portfolio captures; high up-capture and low down-capture is desirable.
A portfolio captures 110% of rising markets and 80% of falling markets.
A high down-capture ratio is desirable.
Consistency
Consistency, shown by rolling returns over many periods, matters more than a single period's return.
A manager's three-year rolling returns beat the benchmark in most windows.
One strong year proves skill.
Standardised reporting
SEBI requires performance of portfolio managers to be reported in a uniform manner, using TWRR, through an independent central performance platform.
Managers' returns can be compared on a common basis.
Each manager may choose its own method.
Gross versus net returns
Gross returns are before fees and expenses while net returns are after them; investors should compare net returns.
An investor looks at returns after costs.
Gross returns are what the client receives.
Style drift
Style drift occurs when a manager moves away from the stated investment approach, which should be monitored.
A large-cap approach quietly buys small caps.
Style drift is the sign of consistent discipline.
Risk-adjusted evaluation
Evaluating a manager involves return, risk, consistency, process and costs, not just headline returns.
An adviser examines several measures before recommending a manager.
Only the last year's return matters.

units.title: Taxation
units.overview: How PMS income is taxed in the client's hands.
facts: Taxation at client level
PMS transactions are in the client's own name, so gains and losses are taxed directly in the client's hands.
Each sale by the manager creates a tax event for the client.
The PMS entity pays tax on behalf of all clients.
Short-term and long-term gains
Gains on listed shares held up to 12 months are short-term and over 12 months long-term, with different tax rates.
A share sold after 14 months gives a long-term gain.
The holding period for listed shares is 36 months.
Dividend income
Dividend received on shares in the portfolio is taxable in the client's hands at the slab rate.
A client adds dividend credited to her account to income.
Dividends are tax-free for all clients.
Capital gains statement
Managers provide a statement of realised gains and losses, which helps the client file her tax return.
A client uses the statement to compute her gains.
No tax statement is provided.
Set-off of losses
Capital losses can be set off against capital gains and carried forward as per the tax law.
A loss on one sale offsets a gain on another.
Losses can never be set off.
Tax on fees
Management fees and expenses may be deductible against gains or income as per the law, subject to conditions.
A client considers the tax treatment of fees paid.
Fees are always deductible.
Turnover and tax
High portfolio turnover can push more gains into short-term, increasing the tax cost.
A manager who trades frequently generates more short-term gains.
Turnover has no tax effect.

units.title: Regulatory, governance and ethical aspects of portfolio managers
units.overview: SEBI's Portfolio Managers Regulations, the conduct of managers and the distributor's duties.
facts: SEBI Portfolio Managers Regulations
These regulations govern registration, conduct, fees, disclosures and client protection for portfolio managers.
A manager's activities are bound by SEBI's rules.
Portfolio managers are free from regulation.
Net worth requirement
A portfolio manager must maintain minimum net worth of ₹5 crore.
A firm falls short on capital and cannot be registered.
A manager needs only ₹10 lakh of net worth.
Fiduciary duty
The manager must act in the client's best interest, with care, diligence and loyalty, and place client interest before its own.
A manager avoids a trade that benefits it at the client's expense.
The manager may favour its own interest.
Prohibition on assured returns
Portfolio managers and distributors cannot assure or guarantee returns on a PMS.
A distributor says 'The PMS will give you 20% every year.'
Distributors may guarantee returns.
Conflict of interest
Managers must disclose and manage conflicts, avoid front running and not misuse client information.
A manager trades ahead of a client's large order.
Front running is acceptable if profit is shared.
Distributor registration
Distributors of PMS must hold the NISM XXI-A certificate and an AMFI ARN, and follow code of conduct.
A distributor completes certification before selling PMS.
Any person can distribute PMS without certification.
Suitability by distributor
The distributor must assess the client's suitability, explain risks and fees and give the disclosure document before onboarding.
A distributor checks a client's risk profile and net worth before recommending PMS.
Suitability is the manager's duty alone.
Commission disclosure
Distributors must disclose commission earned from the portfolio manager to the client.
A distributor tells the client how she is paid.
Commissions are hidden from clients.
Grievance redressal
Clients can complain to the manager, then to SEBI's complaint system, and use online dispute resolution.
An unhappy client files a complaint on the regulator's portal.
Clients have no recourse against portfolio managers.
Penalties
SEBI can penalise, suspend or cancel registration of managers or distributors who violate the regulations.
A manager is penalised for mis-selling.
SEBI cannot act against portfolio managers.
Insider trading
Portfolio managers must not trade on unpublished price-sensitive information, and violations are prosecuted.
A manager buys shares based on confidential merger news.
Insider trading is allowed in managed accounts.
Related-party dealing
Managers must disclose investments in related-party securities and avoid favouring group entities.
A manager discloses its group company's shares in a client's portfolio.
Related-party holdings need not be disclosed.
Code of conduct for distributors
Distributors must act honestly, avoid mis-selling, keep confidentiality and give true information about products.
A distributor refuses to oversell the product's features.
The code allows exaggerated claims.
